speechtext:
Hon J. W. Pickersgill (Bonavisia-Twillingaie): Mr. Speaker, I am rising on a question of privilege. Yesterday a motion was rejected by the house for a copy of the current feasibility study of the proposed causeway between Prince Edward Island and the New Brunswick mainland. I have in my hand a document which has been distributed, I believe, in this house and elsewhere entitled "Northumberland strait crossing, interim report on feasibility study" delivered by Major General H. A. Young, deputy minister of public works, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
I submit that it is an outrageous breach of the privileges of this house to deny to the house something which has subsequently been given to the parliamentary press gallery and to the public generally.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: The hon. member has raised the question as a matter of privilege. If he will recall the events of yesterday, there was a motion made and rejected by the house on its own vote for the production of the document.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Contempt of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: How can parliament be in contempt of parliament?

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on the question of privilege I think there should be some statement made by the government as to the reason for the production of this document in a place other than the House of Commons when the House of Commons was refused it by a vote.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: I find myself in some difficulty about this; because as I recall the practice of the house it does not criticize its own decisions, and in effect what the hon. member is doing by raising this point as a question of privilege is reflecting on the vote which the house took yesterday with respect to the production of this document.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
If Your Honour would permit me to say a word on that point, I am not criticizing the decision the house
took yesterday. I am criticizing the conduct of a member of the government today in producing in this fashion a document that the house decided should not be produced to the house.

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice):
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the minister concerned having just come in he is obviously not in a position te answer at once. Surely, however, it is desirable to recall just what happened yesterday when the motion was made. The minister asked that it stand, and as he explained subsequently, he wanted it to stand because i1 was his view that there was no such document as that technically described by the hon. member's motion. The hon. member, with that facility for precipitate action for which he is so well known, refused to let the motion stand for investigation and forced a vote. In those circumstances the minister had no alternative but to refuse the motion, because he was not at all certain that there was such a document.
Now, what is happening? The hon. member is urging that there is contempt of parliament. It was parliament which decided that the motion should be rejected.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: No.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: It was the House of Commons which decided the motion should be rejected and I fail to see how the House of Commons can be in contempt of itself. It is, therefore, perfectly obvious that if my hon. friends in the opposition would just show a little reasonableness on a request to allow motions to stand, this matter could have been disposed of without the confusion they themselves have generated.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
Since the Minister of Justice has raised this point I would draw Your Honour's attention to the fact that there seems to have been a further breach of the privileges of the house in the statement made by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Walker) yesterday in reply to the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Phillips), because in that statement the minister said categorically that there was no such report, as will be found on page 4001 of Hansard, and today his department issues a report to the parliamentary press gallery. I submit, sir, that no minister of the crown has a right to mislead this house the way the minister did yesterday.

Question of Privilege

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: The statement which has just been made has no foundation in fact. Apparently the rule around here recently is for the opposition regularly to raise smokescreens by way of alleged questions of privilege. This is another example of that type of attitude.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege. The Prime Minister has stated in this house that a statement I made had no foundation in fact.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: This-

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: If the house wants to hear the hon. member there will have to be a little less noise. The hon. member is raising another question of privilege?

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
A question of personal privilege. The Prime Minister, sir, has just stated in this house that a statement I made was not a matter of fact, notwithstanding that the statement I made is right here in Hansard; and I intend, sir, in order to show how irresponsible the conduct of the Prime Minister is, to read this statement.
In reply to a question which the hon. member for Prince directed to the minister after, I might say, this motion had been rejected by the house and which therefore perhaps raises a question of propriety, the minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for directing this question to me, along with preceding questions. While I regret exceedingly that it was not possible to give a reply to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate as to the feasibility or otherwise of the causeway, because it is impossible to do that-we have no such report-
And then today, sir-

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Read on.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: -the parliamentary press gallery is given an interim report on the feasibility study.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: The hon. member has taken a different point of view from that expressed by the Prime Minister on facts which are on the record. It is not possible to continue a debate on a question of privilege unless there is some motion before the house.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: There is no mistake about the statement to which I referred, which was xhat a minister of the crown, the Minister of Public Works, had misled the house.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Look at the record.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Again the Prime Minister is wrong. I did not say he had misled the house. He sought to mislead the house; he did not succeed,

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Order. I must take exception to the last remark of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, that the minister had sought to mislead the house. He knows that such a statement should not stand, and I ask him to withdraw.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I think the minister's words speak for themselves-

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Withdraw.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Be a man and do it quickly.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: -and I would ask the minister to explain how he could say there was no report when he has produced a report today.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Withdraw.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Order. If hon. members will restrain themselves I think the matter might be disposed of. I have asked the hon. member to withdraw the statement that the minister sought to mislead the house.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Ask the Prime Minister to withdraw his smokescreen charge.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Order. I think it would not be in accordance with the standard of conduct we have set for ourselves to allow such a statement to stand. I am sure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, who has a very high appreciation of the practices of parliament, would not want to have that appear in the record. I know that his initial statement referred to a misleading of the house and I take no exception to that, but then he added the other phrase and I think he should amend it.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Your Honour, of course, as almost always, is quite right.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: That is worse.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Shocking condescension.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: In using the words "sought to" I was obviously seeking to interpret the mind of the Minister of Public Works. I would never wish to do that, sir, and I of course withdraw.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: I should like to raise a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I suggest to you, sir, that the Prime Minister should also be asked to withdraw his statement that this matter was raised as a smokescreen and that the statement of the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was not factually correct, inasmuch as the hon. member has read Hansard to show that it was correct. Perhaps the Prime Minister will now withdraw his statement.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: From time to time I have observed that hon. members have used the word "smokescreen" with respect to actions on the other side of the house, and while strictly speaking it is not in order to impute improper motives I do not think that is a statement that I should request be modified unless the hon. member who used it wishes to do so himself.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: He is trying to.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have been on my feet not less than eight times. This matter is simple to everyone except the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. He asked me to table a report.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: No; the word "report" is not in the motion. Read it.

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Why don't you read the motion?

subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
He asked that we should table the current feasibility study in the house. Eventually some day we hope to have a study or report as to the feasibility or otherwise of building a causeway between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. That is what we hope to have, but it is a very difficult, long term project requiring a great deal of research. However, in order to keep the house advised from time to time as to the progress being made progress reports have been made.
These studies involve four or five departments. A great deal of study and research have been put into the matter, including the use of facilities of the national research council. Nevertheless we are not now in a position to give a feasibility report such as was required by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, and it was impossible to table something that we did not have and will not have for some time. I told the house what I would do, and if the hon. member had asked for it we could have done it for him. But he is simply being tipped off by someone, because there are no Liberal representatives from the maritime provinces and therefore he has to do a half-baked job. He does not understand what is going on.
Question of Privilege

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext: Order. I hope the minister who has the floor to deal with a question of privilege will not raise another one.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation; Minister responsible for National Capital Commission
subtopic: MR. PICKERSGILL  FEASIBILITY STUDY, P.E.I.-N.B. CAUSEWAY
speechtext:
Therefore, if he does not know,
I think it is correct to say that we have had two progress reports on the studies that are now going on in connection with this causeway.
In reply to the hon. member I may say that today the hon. member for Prince, who has been following this matter-after all he is a member from Prince Edward Island-has asked for a progress report. I will be very happy to be able to give that report to the house when the orders of the day are reached. This is something entirely different from what was requested by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I do not blame him for not understanding; he very seldom does understand. When the time comes I will make this interim progress report as to our investigations, and then I think even the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate will be able to see the difference between a progress report and a feasibility study, or feasibility report, such as he requested yesterday. The two are so far removed from one another that there should not be any possibility of misunderstanding even by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.

For a copy of the current feasibility study of the proposed causeway between Prince Edward Island and the New Brunswick mainland.
As I told the minister yesterday, the motion was put on the order paper because of a statement in the Charlottetown newspaper. I might point out that the document here is called a feasibility study, and it was quite obvious that this was what was requested.

speechtext: I think both points of view on the question of privilege which the hon. member has raised have been expressed, and the house should proceed to other business.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is inviting associations and individual persons

Inquiries of the Ministry to offer suggestions at this time on the marking of Canada's one hundredth birthday in 1987. Numerous suggestions have already been received from various sources, but the government wishes to be certain that all interested parties and groups have had an opportunity to contribute their ideas.
It might be asked why this invitation is made at this time, some seven years before the actual event. The answer is that activities such as public ceremonies of the nature and magnitude of the ones expected in this country at that time will require years to plan and complete.
It would be unfortunate if any worth-while proposal for the centennial were to be disregarded because it had not come to our attention in time to be included in the overall program or to permit of its execution. As the house knows, a national committee on Canada's centennial comprising ministers and other representatives of the federal government and of the ten provinces has been formed to meet in the early autumn to work out the broad lines of the centennial program. It is suggested, therefore, that if possible any suggestions on the subject should be placed in the hands of the centennial secretariat in the privy council office by August 1.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of Labour whether he is now in a position to reply to the question I addressed to him yesterday.

subtopic: INSTRUCTIONS RESPECTING RELEASE OF FIGURES TO MEMBERS OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Gloucester asked a question in these words:

Can the minister inform the house whether instructions have been issued to the unemployment insurance commission not to divulge to members of parliament unemployment figures available from local or regional offices in their respective areas?
In reply I said that no such instructions had been issued by me and I knew of no instances where hon. members of parliament have been refused unemployment figures. The hon. member for Essex East followed with a supplementary question in the following language:
Has the Minister of Labour given any instructions to the unemployment insurance commission or to any government servant that members of parliament are not to be supplied with information that it has always been regarded as a right of the representatives of the people to have?
In reply I stated:
On the contrary, I have relaxed the practice that had been in force under the previous government.
My reply at this time will be somewhat lengthy and rather detailed. It may be that Your Honour will be of the opinion that my reply is too lengthy to give in answer to a question. If that is the case I would request that I be allowed to deal with this as a question of privilege. The hon. member for Essex East has asked a question which, if it is not answered fully, will leave the impression that I have taken steps to restrict or infringe the privileges of the members of this house. The wording of his question relates to information which he says is regarded as a right of the members of this house. I feel, therefore, that a matter of privilege may be implied here; and the matter is of such importance that it cannot be answered by a simple negative.
Yesterday both the hon. member for Gloucester and the hon. member for Essex East asked me questions about the release of information to members of parliament by the unemployment insurance commission. I have already stated what the hon. member for Gloucester asked, and in reply I said at the time that no such instructions has been issued by me. I feel that I should add that my office has made it known to both regional and local managers that members of parliament are to be supplied on the local level with whatever information is available regarding employment or unemployment in their areas, regardless of the political affiliation of that member. For example, I recently wrote to the managers of the unemployment insurance commission offices at Port Arthur and Fort William in these words:
It would be appreciated if you would supply Mr. D. M. Fisher, M.P., with the figures he requested.

At the same time I should point out that when members of parliament in Ottawa request information from individual employees of the commission, these figures are made available and this information is cleared through my office. I can assure the house that there is nothing new in this practice and I think the reason will be readily understood. I do not think any hon. member would suggest that it would be good administrative practice or in the best interests of the members themselves to have a situation where individual employees of the commission were issuing figures and other information over the telephone on their own authority, particularly in the case of figures or other information which might not yet have been made available to the minister's office.
Let me repeat, Mr. Speaker, that any member of this house will be given whatever information he requests, provided that the information is available and that it is not of a confidential or privileged nature. I would also point out that there are certain recognized procedures and practices of this house which can be followed and which are available to any member in the obtaining of information from the government.
The hon. member for Essex East, in his supplementary question, opened up the general field of information to be supplied by the unemployment insurance commission, when he asked whether I had given instructions that members of parliament were not to be supplied with information which has always been regarded as their right. I am surprised that the hon. member for Essex East, knowing my respect for parliament and for the privileges of members, should have asked that question. I want to provide him with an answer, Mr. Speaker, and in order that there may be no doubt in the minds of hon. members, regardless of where they may sit in the house, I feel that my answer should be as full and complete as possible.
It was brought to my attention in December of 1959 that certain instructions had appeared in the official manuals of the unemployment insurance commission which would have the effect of limiting the availability of information to members of parliament, whether in the provincial or federal legislatures, who were seeking information on behalf of their constituents. I felt that this was an undesirable limitation which was being placed upon members of parliament in carrying out their duties, and I immediately wrote to the commission informing them of my views in this matter.
I do not wish to take up the time of the house unnecessarily, but I feel I should quote
Inquiries of the Ministry briefly from that letter in order that there may be no doubt in the minds of hon. members as to my views. I wrote as follows:
I question the wisdom of this decision. In my opinion, members of the legislative assembly should be afforded every possible courtesy in the offices of the unemployment insurance commission in the same manner as a federal member of parliament.
I went on to say:
When a member of the legislative assembly inquires about a particular case, it is not idle curiosity; it is because he feels that he has an obligation to undertake such action on behalf of his constituents. I feel that any information which would assist a member of the provincial parliament in this objective should be made available to him with all promptitude and courtesy.
It is hardly necessary to say that I hold the same views in regard to members of this house, and that the commission was made aware of those views very early in my administration.
On January 19 I received a letter from the commission explaining why they felt that these restrictions were justified, and I replied on January 20. In my reply I dealt with the situation as it relates to both provincial and federal members of parliament. I would ask the indulgence of the house to refer very briefly to one or two paragraphs in this letter. This is what I wrote on January 20:
I do not see how anything in section 98 could under any circumstances be construed as granting authority for a directive against giving out information to members of parliament.
If there is such a directive, I think it should be rescinded.
On February 4 I was informed by the commission that the instructions had been amended to give effect to the views I had put forward, and to make information available to members of both federal and provincial parliaments who were inquiring on behalf of their constituents. I was also informed that a minute of the commission authorizing the restrictions referred to had been cancelled and that all officers were being advised accordingly.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, to have taken up so much time of the house, but I feel that this is an important matter, reflecting to some extent on the privileges of hon. members, and as such it was proper to deal with it fully.

Mr. Chairman, in this resolution approval is sought of a vote of sums aggregating $600,946,640.92 designed to provide for the expenses of government for the months of June and July. Mr. Chairman, my remarks have to do with Canada's failure to win the 1967 world's fair. This is a dream or vision which has caught the imagination of Canadians in recent months, and here is a sample of the great illusion we had, as shown in an editorial in the Globe and Mail of February 12, 1960:

speechtext:
Would the hon. member permit me to ask him if he does not think it would be more appropriate, instead of raising this matter on a motion for
Interim Supply
the granting of interim supply, to bring it up on the estimates, for instance, of the Postmaster General, as he was the minister principally concerned in the effort to bring this world fair to Montreal? speechtext:
The last time we had a motion for interim supply I think I gave my views on the proper course of debate on such a motion. Of course I do not want to rule any subject out of order unless there is formal objection. If there is agreement on both sides to discuss certain matters, I can see no objection. Interim Supply
agreement that the hon. member can discuss this matter, I have no objection. However, if I am forced to give a ruling I shall do so-

speechtext: I will not do that, but I said if I am forced to give a ruling I will give my views on the subject because I have considered the matter since the last occasion on which it was raised.

I should like to point out that my hon. friend said nothing whatever about bringing forward any grievance. What my hon. friend is discussing is an expenditure which has already been made by the government, very evidently made by the government, and the minister is now asking us to vote money to expend in connection with this precise matter. What the hon. member is seeking to do is to dicuss whether or not the committee is to approve this particular expenditure, which is in the fraction of the total expenditures for the year or part of it for which the Minister of Finance is asking.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate just now said compels me to raise a question of order. I had not done that up to the moment he rose. If what the hon. member for Maison-neuve-Rosemont wishes to discuss is an expenditure already made, then that makes it clearly out of order, because what is sought here is a vote of money for the next two months, the months of June and July. This does not relate at all to expenditures already made. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate has made it quite clear that the subject now raised by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont relates to expenditures hitherto made.

I said part of it had already been made. As the Minister of Finance very well knows, all he is asking for is a fraction. The minister knows as well as I do that the formal reservation of our constitutional rights, which he very solemnly read out a few minutes ago, does reserve all those rights so far as current expenditures in the current fiscal year are concerned. I concede that it would be quite wrong to discuss some expenditure made in the fiscal year now closed, but this is an expenditure being made at the present time. It is a continuing process throughout the year. The money is taken out of some vote; I do not know which vote, but it is obviously taken out of some vote. Surely, therefore, it is completely within the competence of the representatives of the taxpayers here, who are being asked to vote the money, to discuss whether or not is should be voted.
[The Chairman.]

speechtext: What is the view of the committee? In their minds is there any limitation to the discussion in circumstances like these? Is it a fact that any subject that may have any relevance to an item of the estimate is in order?
Discussion in unlimited.

speechtext: Is it unlimited? I should like to hear the views of the committee on that.

It has certainly become well established over the years that on this motion for interim supply members have a right to discuss every subject concerning any estimate or any appropriation. In other words they have a right to discuss any subject which they could discuss under the estimates of a department. The minister will certainly accept that interpretation of the rules, because he will remember very well that in 1956, on a motion for interim supply, there was a debate on the conduct of the Speaker which extended for hour after hour. The only justification under the rules for that debate was that there was an item in the estimates covering the salary of the Speaker.
The minister will also remember that in 1957 he took some six pages of Hansard on this kind of motion to discuss a matter which had no direct relevance to any particular item, but which was considered to be in order. That is all we are endeavouring to do at this time, to carry out a well established rule of the House of Commons which permits us to bring up matters of expenditure in the way my hon. friend is trying to do now.

If I may speak to this point of order, I should like to point out that on a motion for interim supply in the year 1957 Messrs. Knight, Knowles, Fleming, Stewart, Hees, Hamilton (Notre Dame de Grace) and Diefenbaker spoke. In addition, Mr. Ellis spoke on bulletin No. 10 which related to the Department of National Revenue, and Mr. Diefenbaker spoke on the question of keeping open the customs port of West Poplar, Saskatchewan.
On a motion for interim supply in 1956 the then leader of the opposition spoke in regard to pipe lines. Mr. Knowles spoke; Mr. Drew also spoke on the subject of reform of the other place; Mr. Knowles spoke on closure; Mr. Blackmore spoke on the Bank of Canada; Mr. Hees spoke on pipe lines; Mr. Diefenbaker spoke on Right Hon. Mr. Howe's radio speech; Mr. Cameron spoke; Mr. Barnett spoke on fishing and combines; Hon. William Hamilton spoke-he was not "honourable" then-on the tax on

Since I do not know of a better time than today, at which to raise this matter, Mr. Chairman, with your permission I will continue my remarks. Before going on with them, however, I wish to express the hope that the time taken by this discussion will not be included as part of my allotted time.
There will not be a world's exhibition in Montreal in 1967. The question now arises as to what happened to deprive us of a feast so well earned by all Canadians for this centennial year of confederation. In other words, where lies the responsibility for such spectacular and disappointing failure or blunder in Paris on May 5? This is a question I will try to examine in as many aspects as possible in the relatively short time at my disposal.
At the outset, let us recall that the city of Montreal was pledging $5 million of its own in this project, the Quebec government $15 million, and that the federal government had promised to add $20 million in order to provide for a grand total of $40 million.
On February 8, 1960, at the inaugural meeting of the provisional national committee of Canada's centennial, the Montreal bid and proposal was approved by the Canadian government and was approved by all parties in the House of Commons later on. This was therefore a national proposition under the direct and immediate responsibility of the government, as we can see if we refer to page 918 of Hansard of February 10, 1960:
The cabinet has approved the appointment of the Postmaster General as the minister to represent the government in relation to the plans for this project.
Hon. members will recall that on March 8, in Paris, the U.S.S.R. prevented a vote as between Canada and Austria, and how it was agreed to postpone a deciding vote to May 5,

1960. But before going any further I should like to put on Hansard a few articles from a book entitled "Dominion of Canada Treaty Series," 1934, more especially from the chapter entitled "Convention Relating to International Exhibitions" agreed in Paris, November 22, 1928 by 31 countries including Canada. Let us read articles 35, 36 and 39.
Article 35
(a)	At any time after the coming into force of the present convention any non-signatory country may accede thereto.
(b)	Such accession may be effected by a notification in writing transmitted through the diplomatic channel to the French government. Such notifications of accession shall be deposited in the archives of that government.
(c)	The French government shall transmit immediately to the governments of all signatory and acceding countries certified copies of any such notifications, showing the dates on which they were received.
Article 36
The present convention shall come into force, in respect of the countries which have taken part in the first deposit of ratifications, one month after the date of the proces-verbal thereof. In the case of countries which ratify subsequently or accede thereto, and in respect of colonies, protectorates, overseas territories and territories under suzerainty or mandate not included in ratifications, the convention shall take effect one month after the date of receipt of the notifications provided for in articles 33, paragraph (d); 34, paragraph (b); 35, paragraph (b) .. .
Article 39
The government of the French republic shall communicate to the international bureau copies of all ratifications, accessions and denunciations.
If Russia was not a member of the international bureau before February, 1960, having in mind the provisions of articles 35, 36 and 39 it would be most interesting to know exactly at what date the notification of Russia was received by the French government and then filed with the international bureau. We would therefore be able to appreciate what was the delay that elapsed between the notification by Russia of membership and March 8, which was the date fixed for the deciding vote as between Canada and Austria.
The reason for this is obvious. If we refer to the official letter from the U.S.S.R. ambassador in Paris to the international bureau, we note that this letter is dated February 26, 1960. I hold in my hand a copy of this letter which was printed in La Presse in its edition of March 15, 1960. It reads as follows:
Paris, February 26, 1960.
(Translation):
International Exhibitions Bureau.
This letter is over the signature of the Russian ambassador.
I am instructed to inform you that the government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics intends to organize the next universal exposition of the first category in 1967 in Moscow, capital of the Soviet union.

The Soviet union is in a position to organize and hold an exhibition of a high and proper standard, strictly in accordance with the provisions of the 1928 Convention relating to international exhibitions.
The government of the Soviet union expresses the hope that the holding of the universal exhibition for the first time on U.S.S.R. territory will constitute an important step toward the subsequent development of international co-operation and mutual understanding between all nations.
Since the government of the Soviet union intends to start preparing at once for this international event, it would be grateful if governments of the 1928 convention contracting countries were immediately informed Of the Soviet government's plan and if the 1967 universal exhibition in Moscow was duly registered by the international bureau.
I should be obliged to you for acknowledging receipt of this letter.
(Text):
According to information I could gather from press reports, Russia argued that her application should be entertained on March 8 because this application was made within a period of six months after the first official application of Austria, which was filed in November, 1959. Again, after examining the contention of the U.S.S.R. and the provisions of this constitution on international fairs, I fail to see in the constitution any ground sustaining such contention. At any rate, Russia became a competitor on February 26, 1960 and it would be interesting to know why the Canadian people were not notified of this development until March 8 when this was announced in La Presse and we were told that Moscow was now in the competition to obtain this international exhibition.
You will recall, Mr. Chairman, that according to the provisions of the constitution, article 29, which I read a few minutes ago, it is laid down that notification of accessions is to be filed with the international bureau by the French government. Thus, this application from Russia late in February should not have been overlooked by the Canadian government.
Let us deal at this point with the deciding factor-the vote taken on May 5. We all know that on March 8 there were 23 countries-members of the international bureau-with the right to vote. The Canadian Press received, apparently on or around April 25, 1960, the astounding news that seven iron curtain countries had joined the international bureau and would have the right to vote on May 5. This was astonishing news for the Canadian public as a whole, but it should have been no surprise to the Canadian government if members of the government had been on their toes. Had they studied a very peculiar paragraph on page 15 of the constitution under the heading "protocol of signature", I submit the Canadian government might have found there

in black and white the pattern followed by the U.S.S.R. even though this protocol was signed as long ago as 1928. I quote:
The delegation of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics declares that, in the application of the provisions of article 4 of the convention, whereby an interval of at least five years must elapse between two special exhibitions of the same kind organized in the same country, the government of the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics reserves the right to regard as separate countries the six republics members of the union-
There follows the names of the republics which Russia claims should be recognized as entities, each having the right to vote.
It would therefore be interesting to know:
1.	What is the date of the application of each of the seven iron curtain countries for membership in the bureau as shown in the files lodged with the French government?
2.	At what date were the seven notifications transmitted through the diplomatic channel of the French government to the international bureau, and when was Canada informed of the same?
3.	Did the Canadian government check to see whether in respect to the seven iron curtain countries the provisions of the constitution had been strictly adhered to?
If the right to vote of these seven iron curtain countries was justified-which I doubt-then another question is raised, namely why did we not do the same? We must not forget that between February 26, the date of the entrance of Russia, and May 5, the date of the deciding vote, there was ample time in which we might have persuaded friendly countries to join the bureau, and any suggestion that the Canadian government was taken by surprise is not supported by the facts. In this connection I wish to quote an editorial which appeared in the Gazette of May 6, 1960:
In fact, Russia herself was not a member of this organization until three months ago; she entered in February. But once she decided to come in, she was determined to have what she was seeking. For this reason she made the necessary arrangements-all quite legally-to bring into the bureau seven of the nations of the Soviet bloc. They are Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Poland, Roumania, Bulgaria and the two Soviet republics of Byelorussia and the Ukraine.
It is an old technique-as old as the hills. It is the method of joining some organization and bringing your supporters in with you.
If Canada failed in these negotiations in Paris, she failed because she did not counter Russia's move. As this was a tough game, perhaps it ought to have been played more toughly.
As Canada's Department of External Affairs had some part in the matter, it was in a position to supply information on Russia's plan to bring in her seven voters. Perhaps such information was given by the department but was not acted upon. For Canada might well have persuaded other countries of the non-Communist world to enter also.
Interim Supply
There are many such countries. They are even to be found within the commonwealth; Australia is one.
We have been outmatched and outguessed, and what surprises me most is the fact that on March 11 we had been warned by no other than his worship, the mayor of Montreal, that if we wished to succeed more planning was necessary and urgent. While I am on the subject, may I recall that we were also informed in March through reliable sources, namely, the representative of Belgium, that the official application submitted on behalf of Canada was not acceptable because it was not labeled in conformity with the requirements of the regulations. In connection with this point I will read article 8 which prescribes as follows:
Such applications shall state the title of the exhibition and its duration, and shall be accompanied by the classification of exhibits, copies of the general regulations, the jury regulations, and all documents necessary to show the measures proposed to ensure the safety of persons and property, the protection of industrial property and copyright, and to satisfy the conditions prescribed below in Sections IV and V.
According to the same reliable source, this would have been the real reason for the postponement of the deciding vote from March 8 to May 5, 1960.
These are the facts, and I submit that the responsibility for this spectacular failure or blunder lies directly with this government. We have missed the boat again, due to lack of leadership and due to the confusion and fumbling of the government which has shown a complete lack of interest, imagination and vision with regard to this matter. What took place in Paris in respect to this world exhibition was nothing less than a political election at international level. The poor result we obtained is to be regretted and resented by Canadians as a whole and by Montrealers in particular.

speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
have just a brief observation or two to make on this subject. I agree, I think, with only one part of one sentence of the remarks just made by the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont. I myself feel it is regrettable that Canada was not chosen to be the host of the world's fair, but there we part. The hon. member has built up his observations on a basis of newspaper clippings, hearsay and other material.
For example, the hon. member was quoting from a book published in 1934 without realizing that the convention was rewritten and revised in 1948. However, I have no argument with the main points he has brought up. They are contained in the new convention as well.

Interim Supply
Basically, the situation is this. First of all the hon. member cast doubt on the acceptability of our application. The answer is that the application was completely acceptable in every way. There was no change made in it between March 8 and May 5 and it was this application which was voted on. Any suggestion to the contrary is completely and absolutely without foundation. This is proved by the fact that it was accepted by the organization and voted upon.
There are two other points basic to the argument the hon. gentleman raised. We can deal with these quite simply. The hon. member said, "What about the seven countries that came in? Why did you not do something about it?" The answer is, according to his own information, that in order to vote on May 5 they required to be members of the bureau by April 5. Their accessions actually were made between March 30-that is six days before the final date-and April 4 which is one day before the final date, one day before the required time. The hon. member may be interested to know that we did not receive official notification of the accessions from the French government until May 2 which is almost a month after they joined the bureau. It takes some time for information to find its way through normal diplomatic channels. The reason the Canadian Press had the story on April 25 was that in our constant efforts to keep abreast of all developments in connection with the fair we had ourselves turned up through diplomatic channels news of these accessions and had taken steps to confirm the fact long before we received any official advice whatever. I may say that under these circumstances it is obvious that we could not rush in at the last moment, within the last six days, to counter a move such as that.
Finally, the hon. member asked, "why did you not do something like this beforehand?" I would suggest to him that there has been in many parts of the world surprise and I might almost say dismay at the particular course of action which was followed by these satellite states in this connection. International bodies of this sort which are not major political bodies but organizations which are set up to regulate, control and direct some small section of international relations are not normally a battleground for one country as against another. They are designed primarily to come to thoughtful decisions and bring the benefit of the wisdom of their membership to bear on these matters. Under these circumstances countries find their way in, after adequate notice, one or two at a time. They are not introduced to swing a

vote as was done in this particular case. This certainly would not be the approach of the free nations of the world, I am quite sure.
I might point out to the hon. gentleman that the free nations of the world under our democratic process are not able to line up, whip into line and rush in almost overnight, other countries. The free nations of the world make their own decisions. They consider these matters carefully, slowly and deliberately. To suggest that on such short notice we would be required to introduce a number of nations to offset those that entered is to exhibit a complete non-recognition of the facts in this particular instance.
I close simply by saying that throughout this operation there has been a tremendous effort exerted. I am told by those in the Department of External Affairs it has been one of the strongest efforts that has ever been put forward in anything of this sort over a long time in an attempt to bring this fair to Canada. Every stone has been turned, every effort has been made and every person has been contacted who seemed in any way able to assist us. When you examine the results you will find that they hinged on the sudden entry of a group of nations satellite to the U.S.S.R. Without these last minute entries for the countering of which there was no course of action open to us Canada would have led in every vote which was taken and that, I suggest, is the measure of the worth of the effort we put forth.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the Postmaster General a question. In view of the-what shall I call it-sharp practice followed by the Soviet union in introducing six satellites at the last minute, as it were, in the last month, and in view of the delay on the part of the French government, which may be understandable, in making that change known to the Canadian government, would it have been possible or desirable to ask the French government whether under those circumstances the meeting could have been postponed?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think we could have done that within the rules of the bureau. The bureau sets its own meetings. The French government acts purely as the repository of these accessions and transmits them to other bodies. They have no control whatever over the activities of the bureau itself.
Could we have asked the bureau?

One
could suggest that it would have been possible to ask the bureau but this meeting had been established long in advance. It had been set for the definite purpose of voting on

this and I suggest there was no other course of action open to us but to proceed with the meeting as called.
What was the reason for the first postponement?

am glad the hon. gentleman asked that question because here again the hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rosemont was somewhat in error. According to the regulations of the bureau six months must elapse or can elapse between the first application of a nation and the time that that application is voted on and at any time during the six months period other nations can enter their applications. Canada entered hers and was quite prepared to have the vote taken at the March 8 meeting. Russia came in just a few days before that meeting and took the position that she insisted on having the full six months elapse before the vote was taken.

Would the minister permit me a question at this point? Was the Canadian delegation accompanied by a legal adviser in Paris? I question the validity of the reason brought by Russia for postponing the election which was to take place in March. I say that because I fail to see in the constitution anything that sustains Russia's point of view that six months must elapse after the filing of the first applications. Was the delegation accompanied by a legal officer?

Mr. Chairman, you do not need a legal adviser to
appreciate most of these points. The answer to the hon. member's question is no, we did not have a legal adviser, but this point was fully considered both by our own delegation and the bureau generally and the course of action which was followed was arrived at as a result of those discussions.

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, in order to make the record clear, may I say this. The minister said I was citing extracts from an old convention dated 1928. This is true but unfortunately I forgot to say that I am citing from the new version amended in 1934 which is the one that is up to date.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct my remarks to an item of interest that has been in most of our newspapers during the last week or two. I refer to the disastrous floods in the northern Ontario area and particularly the floods at Mount Joy township which is across the river from the town of Timmins.
As most hon. members know, a total of something like 2,000 people had to be evacuated because of the flood. I wish some hon.
Interim Supply
members could see just how extensive is the damage in that township. In fact, Mr. Chairman, I should like to extend an invitation to members on both the government side and the Liberal opposition side, if they are free, to come up when I go home this week end and see at first hand some of the damage that exists up there. In some cases logs have been driven right through windows and have beaten about inside the house for a period of four or five days. Stoves are ruined as are refrigerators and all sorts of household equipment, and in particular furnaces with their electric motors, and everything of that nature. As most hon. members will realize, a furnace is a very necessary implement up in the northland.
The damage is both direct and indirect. Many of the farms are flooded to such an extent that there is very little hope of any crop this year. Many of the farmers lost livestock. In other cases where the houses themselves were not flooded, the sewers backed up in the basements and flooded the basements. Pumps were put to work. When the people had to be evacuated the pumps could not be properly attended and when the people came back they found that the pumps had drawn up sand and so forth underneath so that the foundations of the houses had dropped and in some instances extensive repairs are required to most buildings.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Has the hon. member any idea of the numbers of cattle that were lost?

I have no idea of the total; I know that on one farm one farmer lost eight of his purebred Jersey cows but I have no idea of the total loss. I do know that for a period of three days the only way they could get feed in and milk out was by helicopter. An R.C.A.F. helicopter was moved in to assist and it did yeoman service in that particular field.
As some hon. members know, they have started a flood disaster fund and the Ontario provincial government has offered to match dollar for dollar. If and when the federal government has an opportunity to assist in this matter I should like them to give the lead in something that is very necessary.
The low lying section of Mount Joy township, which runs right along the river, has been built up in a place where it should never have been built up at all. It is subject to floods in any spring when the water is slightly higher than usual and much more so at a -time of major floods such as we have had this year. I think it is rather a matter

Interim Supply
of throwing good money after bad to spend extensive amounts to repair those houses. Anyone who has seen the result of flooding knows that floors are buckled and plaster falls from the walls. It would take extensive repairs to put those houses back into proper condition. Just a matter of two or three hundred yards away there is a steady rise and there are millions of acres all across the north country where those houses could have been built, or where families could be moved, and we would have a permanent cure to this thing and not a temporary one. If we make temporary improvements we may have to go through the same thing in two or three years' time.
I have discussed this with the minister's officials in the township and they are fully in accord with this. If and when the federal officials consider some financial assistance I should like this suggestion to be kept in mind and posibly we might be able to find a permanent cure for this problem rather than a temporary one.
I should like to mention the desperate condition of the township itself. In the part that was flooded this year there is, I am told, approximately 80 per cent of the assessable property. Anyone who is familiar with municipal affairs knows that when a municipality is just about to send out its tax bills for the year and finds itself faced with a flooded area of 80 per cent of its assessable property it finds itself really in desperate financial straits.
The picture of assistance locally was something that would warm the heart of anyone who saw it. Immediately the call went out, the danger was realized, and every hall in the town of Timmins, the Red Cross, the Salvation Army, all the parish, all the church halls, everything, were placed at the disposal of those victims, and when they were evacuated they were promptly rounded up, fed and clothed where necessary. The spirit of the community was such that by the end of the week those halls were empty because all -the refugees had been taken into private homes throughout the township.
The provincial government moved in and set up a mobile welfare unit which would look after all the needs in regard to food and clothing for -the victims until they were rehabilitated. This, of course, is on the normal 40-20-20 basis, 40 per cent by the federal government, 20 per cent by the provincial government and 20 per cent by the municipality. As I mentioned a moment ago, the greatest difficulty will be for the municipality

to find the 20 per cent because of the condition in which it finds itself at -the present time.
The response to the disaster fund has been most remarkable. All the local papers, the radio stations, the television stations have done a tremendous job. I recall watching the local television station, CFCL, Friday night. They put on a live program for one hour, with all the big local entertainers donating their time. They asked the people to phone in requests and to phone in their donations. In that one hour they raised over $2,500 in donations. They got donations from as far away as Rouyn, Noranda, Cobalt, Kapuskasing and Hearst.
There is one problem that really came to light in this emergency as no doubt it has in other emergencies which have struck as quickly as this one. I refer to the lack of coordination among the various people who want to help. There were numerous occasions when people were standing by ready to assist but because of the lack of co-ordination their help went unused. I do not think blame for this can be put on any one individual. The head of the local civil defence coordination, who is incidentally the fire chief, worked day and night in an attempt to coordinate all the various offers of assistance, and so forth. I think the problem was caused by the lack of understanding and lack of realization of the public generally in regard to civil defence. I know that over the years the fire chief has tried to get the people in that area interested in civil defence. In fact, in the township of Mount Joy he made many efforts to get some people interested in the need and use of civil defence.
This may be something for the minister and for the civil defence in general to consider. They should consider a possible change of name. If it were called civil emergency rather than civil defence it might appeal more to and get more people interested in it and act. When we talk about civil defence to the general public they immediately get a picture of evacuations because of an atom bomb or something of that nature. In a place like Timmins, of course, the people feel that they would be one of the last targets in an atom bomb attack. They think that it will never happen to them. But I believe that every community across the country is in fear of something. One community is in fear of floods, another in fear of bush fires and another has some other danger hanging over it. If civil defence could be related to the particular problem of the community it is possible that we could get people interested,

and once they became interested a much better job could be done so far as civil defence co-ordination is concerned.
Finally, once again I should like to extend an invitation to any hon. members of the house who are interested to come to Timmins this week end. I should like particularly to see a cabinet minister or parliamentary assistant come along with the group.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to take much of the time of the committee and I hope what I have to say will not be very contentious. I wish to say at once that I am going to be critical of a public agency but in doing so I am not implying any criticism whatever of the government.
I asked a question in the house the other day which was answered by the Minister of National Revenue. It had to do with the regulations of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, if they had any, with respect to persons being candidates for public office. The minister's answer appears on page 3954 of Hansard for May 17, at which time he said:
I am informed by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that section 8, subsection 3 of the bylaws of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation states:
''No officer or employee of the corporation employed on a full-time basis shall be a candidate for any public elective office or actively support any candidate for any public elective office, but an officer or employee of the corporation may, subject to the permission of the president, be or actively support a candidate for a municipal or civic office, provided that the acceptance of or the support of the candidature for such office does not interfere with the proper and regular performance of his duties with the corporation."
I do not think it would be fair to the committee or to the minister to debate the general question involved in this bylaw. I must say that I do not know when the bylaw was passed. It may have been there since the inception of the corporation, but I was never aware of it before. I admit that right oft. I do think it does raise a pretty fundamental question.
I am troubled, as I am sure every hon. member of the house is, by the extent to which private employers not directly but indirectly limit the capacity of citizens to offer themselves for public service, and it seems to me that unless there is some very compelling reason for it employees of public corporations should not be put in the position that civil servants properly are but should be in the same position as employees of the C.N.R. with respect to candidature of this kind.
I admit at once that there are some special problems connected with broadcasting that would have to be taken into account but, as 79951-0-255

I say, it is not to discuss the general principle involved that I am saying what I am saying now. The minister went on to say with reference to a particular case which has arisen recently in British Columbia:
In reply to the supplementary question relating to the one particular individual mentioned, I am advised by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation that this supplementary question, which related to British Columbia, refers to the case of a commentator on the program "Neighbourly News" who was not a member of the staff but a freelance artist and who announced his candidacy in the next British Columbia election. The person in question has, I understand, been adopted as a candidate in an election which undoubtedly will take place in the province of British Columbia but which has not been called. It seems to me this is of some importance even with relation to the bylaw. Moreover, the bylaw, of course, applies to full-time employees and not to persons who are employed at piecework as this particular person had been.
It does seem to me that there are, in the facts of this case, certain circumstances which seem to suggest that the action taken was neither fair nor reasonable, nor is it the kind of action which any of us who believe in our free and representative institutions should wish to see taken. It so happens that this gentleman is a member of the party to which I belong, but it would not make any difference to me to what party he belonged. In the case of people who are simply employed to do a particular specific thing once a week, it seems to me it is wrong to say that these people cannot be adopted as candidates for some future election and retain their engagement. If they use the opportunity given to them to broadcast in order to further their candidature or to further the particular interests of their party, I quite agree that would be an abuse and if that were done I think the corporation would be perfectly justified in dealing with it as an abuse.
But in this particular case this man has been compiling and broadcasting a program called "Neighbourly News" for 15 years. There is a similar program on the radio here. I listen to it occasionally on Sunday morning, as I am sure some other hon. members do, and a more completely non-political program it would be pretty hard to imagine. I quite grant that it might be possible to introduce into it something that would be objectionable or unfair, but surely under our system we should not anticipate that someone is going to do something wrong.

probably wrote to you.

That is quite true. The gentleman himself wrote it. I have the document sent by him and I would be very glad to read any part or all of it into the record or show it to the parliamentary secretary. If the rules permitted I would, of course, be quite happy to lay it on the table but only ministers can lay documents on the table as I well know from previous experience.
This gentleman, who is in every way a reputable person, was in fact, according to the information supplied to me, told in the first instance very shortly before he was to give his broadcast that he was not going to be allowed to go on and it was only after he had protested that he was then told he could go on for another two weeks. He was also given permission to make a farewell broadcast. According to the information given to me, which I believe to be correct, every script that he used was always read in advance by someone else.
There would have been, therefore, very little opportunity for him to abuse this broadcast in any case. He was told that he could make a farewell broadcast. I have a copy of the text here of the speech he was going to make. Part of the text was censored and the person in the C.B.C. who censored it signed it and initialled it. I will not read the whole thing, but will read the part he was told to leave out. Perhaps I will have to read the previous sentence so that the continuity will be clear.
And now, neighbours, it's not going to be easy for me to say what I am now going to tell you. This is my last Neighbourly News broadcast. You might say this is my swan song as your Sunday morning reporter of the doings of the small towns and their folks, and yes, even their dogs and cats and other pets.
That part was left in, and this is the part that was to be struck out:

On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; I am just wondering whether the hon. gentleman would not agree that this is strictly a matter of internal management of the corporation. This house would not expect to have the handling of the day to day affairs of the corporation nor matters of staff policy. I am just wondering whether this material which the hon. member is trying to put on the record is really relevant and proper at this time.

I think the parliamentary secretary did not hear what I said at the outset of my remarks, through no fault of his own, because he did not know I was going to speak on this subject and he did not happen to be in the chamber. What I said was that I felt a fundamental human right was involved here, the right of a citizen to be adopted as a candidate for the legislature or for any other public office without having a penalty put upon him by a public corporation. It is that matter of fundamental human rights, which according to the speech from the throne are certainly within the purview of this parliament, upon which I am speaking. We are being asked to vote a very considerable sum of money for the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation which is ultimately responsible, not to the government but to parliament.
I would raise a question, and I only raise it as a question, as to whether the statute does, in fact, give the corporation power to do things of this sort, which do seem to call into question a person's civil rights. This is not a matter of any internal management, this is a matter of public privilege, because the corporation was not seeking to discipline somebody for some infraction but because the corporation, by its action was, in fact, penalizing someone in the exercise of his undoubted civic rights; that is the point I wish to make. If the parliamentary secretary feels that there is still a point of order I would be glad to sit down so Your Honour could rule.

I have just this observation. While the hon. member may question, on broad lines, the principle that he enunciated, I am wondering whether or not he is going too far in going into the detail of what had been taken out of the talk. That has nothing to do with the question. I have not got the act before me, but it will be remembered that it is clearly indicated in the legislation that matters of staff policy shall be for the president of the corporation; that is what it says.
This gentleman was not a member of the staff of the C.B.C.

It is really a legal nicety, I think, to indicate whether or not a person

is a staff member when he is a full-time employee, a regular part-time commentator engaged on a contract or when he is an occasional commentator hired on a strictly free-lance basis. The dividing line as between a regular part-time commentator under contract and a full-time employee is extremely narrow. It is for that reason I am raising this point of order as to whether it is appropriate to discuss matters of staff policy of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation in this committee.

Perhaps before Your Honour makes a decision I could cite a very distinguished precedent. A question arose on a matter of interim supply on March 29, 1957, with respect to a part-time commentator on the C.B.C., and it was debated at some length in this committee. One of the distinguished participants in that debate was the Minister of Finance. It does seem to me, sir, that what is sauce for the goose should be sauce for the gander.
As to the other point raised by the parliamentary secretary as to whether or not it is a proper thing for me to read the part of this document that was censored, I think perhaps, in a way, the parliamentary secretary may have a point there. There is no question in this case but that this man, under the terms of his contract, did submit his scripts for censorship. They were always submitted and, therefore, I assume that if this particular passage were to be cut out, he would have no very valid complaint on that ground if he was being continued in his employment. But this, after all, was not a broadcast in a series. He was being permitted by the C.B.C. to give a farewell broadcast when his employment was terminated. Then, that farewell broadcast was butchered, and it seemed to me that that was a rather serious thing.
It seems to me, also, that perhaps more than any other assembly in this country, this House of Commons should be jealous of the civil rights of others, particularly those who are seeking to be candidates for public af-fice.

My reason and my justification for raising it at this time and taking up the time of the committee in order to do so is that I feel it is extremely important, if we are going to maintain our free representative institutions, that as few obstacles as possible be put in the way of a citizen offering himself for public service in an elective capacity. It seems to me that public corporations should set an example to the rest of the country in this regard in the right way and not what seems to me to be the wrong way. In saying that I do not want anyone to misinterpret for a minute what I have to say and to suggest that I am saying that people who are candidates should be allowed to go on broadcasting during an election campaign or that they should broadcast at all if they are broadcasting the kind of broadcast in which there would be abuse. I would not suggest that for a moment.

There is also another broadcasting matter I wish to say a brief word about. It does not affect the C.B.C.; it affects the board of broadcast governors. Here again another important principle is involved. I do not intend to go into details in this case. This matter also was the subject of a question on the order paper. It was question No. 359 and appeared in Hansard of May 9, 1960. The questions I asked were as follows:
1.	Was a broadcast entitled "What are the national issues in the west coast union fight" broadcast by station CJOR, Vancouver, on February 20, 1960?
The answer given was yes. The second question was as follows:
2.	If so, was station CJOR forbidden by the board of broadcast governors to permit the rebroadcast of this program on other stations and, if so, for what reason?
The answer given was as follows:
Station CJOR, Vancouver, was advised that the program could not be rebroadcast until the board received assurances from the station that those holding views opposed to those expressed on the program of February 20, 1960 would be given an equal opportunity to express these views on the first possible program following.
The step taken by the board in this instance was consistent with the provisions of the board's directive to all radio stations entitled "Political and controversial broadcasting policies." This directive requires that, if a station broadcasts a program on a controversial subject, equal opportunity must be given to all parties to the controversy to express their views. After listening to the taped recording of the program broadcast by station CJOR on February 20, entitled "What Are the National Issues in the West Coast Union Fight", the board was satisfied that this requirement had not been met.
I am not going to take any time on that matter. With that general principle I thoroughly approve. I think one of the best features of broadcasting in Canada is that in connection with these controversial broadcasts we have a general regulation to provide for the airing of both sides. The last thing I would ever do would be to attack that principle in which I firmly believe. But in this particular case I think the board of broadcast governors made a mistake. If the facts are as they have been represented to me- and again I may say I have made every effort to find out-a real effort was made in this case to get persons to represent both sides of the case more than a week beforehand but unfortunately, though there was every prospect that this opportunity would be accepted, the person to represent one side did not turn up. It was a broadcast from a meeting and the meeting had to be held. It

seems to me that every reasonable opportunity had been given. I think that here again we should always err-if there is going to be any erring at all-on the side of liberality and of freedom rather than the reverse.

I want to go along with most of the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. In a case like this I feel it is far better to err on the side of leniency than to be too rigid in the application of the rule that people engaged politics should not be in the employ of the C.B.C.
In Saskatchewan we have, of course, a bill of rights; and in that province civil servants have the right under the law to take a normal citizen's part in political activities as long as it is not within their working hours. However, we also have another rule which provides that anyone who becomes a political candidate shall immediately leave the position which he or she occupies, but can obtain leave of absence for the period of the election or during the time the person concerned is a candidate. We feel that in a democracy such as ours it is the duty of the government to preserve the fundamental right of citizens to take part in politics and afford them some protection in their normal occupations.
