speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENT OF PENSION DURING ABSENCE FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I think the purpose of this resolution is generally understood, but I should perhaps say a few words about it, reserving, of course, the details until the amending bill has been introduced and we have the text of it before us for debate on second reading.
When the Old Age Security Act was first introduced in 1951 it was considered by the government of the day that payments of pension to persons 70 years of age and over with the required residence qualifications should be limited to those periods of time when the pensioners themselves were actually living in Canada. This was in accordance with the provisions which had been in effect for over 20 years in the legislation which preceded the Old Age Security Act-namely, the original old age pensions act. Accordingly, the Old Age Security Act, as originally approved by parliament in 1951, provided that whenever an old age security pensioner left Canada his pension was automatically suspended for the period of his absence, subject, of course, to immediate resumption on his return. In all such cases, of course, the pensioner was entitled to his pension for the month of his departure and the month of his return.
In addition, section 5 (1) of the original Old Age Security Act went a little further by providing that the pensioner on his return might also be entitled to pick up his pension payments for a period of three months during which he was absent in any calendar year, provided that he returned to Canada within six months from the date of his departure.
At the time the law was first passed little if any objection was taken to the provision that I have described, and there were possibly good and valid reasons for such a restriction at the time. The new legislation

Old Age Security Act
was being placed on a quasi contributory basis, and everyone living in Canada was, modities, as well as an additional 2 per per cent sales tax on purchases of most commodities, as well as an additional two per *cent income tax levy on taxable income in order to help finance the new old age security payments. In addition to these levies, the corporation tax was also increased by an additional two percentage points at that time. Since these additional levies for old age security purposes were all initiated in 1952 no one could claim that because of contributions paid during an earlier period he had built up any acquired rights which would justify the expectation that he should carry his pension with him if he moved outside of Canada. Anybody moving to reside outside of Canada automatically ceased to pay any of the old age security levies I have mentioned, and consequently he could hardly expect to continue to receive an old age security benefit outside of Canada to which he had not previously contributed. In this context the initial provision for three months of permissible absence-in addition to the month of departure and the month of return -without forfeiture of pension was probably reasonably fair at that time, since it permitted persons to leave the country for visits of short duration and to spend the more severe winter months in warm climates, with automatic reinstatement of benefits on return to Canada and with little if any loss in respect of the periods of absence.
As the years have passed, however, individuals have begun to build up what might be described as acquired rights through contributions which they have paid through extra income or sales tax levies over a period which is now approximately eight years in duration. More and more, as time passes, these individuals come to feel that they have contributed to their pension through their working years; that it should be regarded as their retirement benefit as a matter of right; and that they should therefore not be required to forfeit their old age security benefit when they leave the country. In the view of many people, the provisions which were put in the Old Age Security Act in the first place, however justifiable they may have been at that time, are now coming to work a certain amount of hardship and unfairness on individual Canadians who have contributed to the old age security fund for a good many years and who now feel that when they reach the age of 70 and qualify for old age security benefits they should be free to take their pensions with them wherever they go.
It will be recalled that the government first reviewed this matter in 1957, shortly after
IMr. Monteith (Perth).]
it took office following the June, 1957 election. At that time the Old Age Security Act had been in effect only five and a half years. The rates of contribution were still based on the original 2-2-2 formula, and the maximum old age security contribution for any year under the 2 per cent income tax levy could not exceed $60. Consequently, apart from the amount of sales tax contributed by any individual for old age security purposes, no one at that time had contributed to the old age security fund, through the income tax levy, more than $300, or the equivalent of less than eight months of old age security benefit at the $40 rate then prevailing. Accordingly, while the government at that time decided that there should be some relaxation of the existing restrictions on the movement of pensioners outside of Canada, it did not feel that the time had yet arrived when it could recommend the full recognition of the principle that old age security pensioners should take their pensions with them where-ever they went outside of Canada. In consequence, the government recommended, and parliament approved, an amendment to section 5 of the Old Age Security Act extending from three months to six months the period for which a pensioner returning to Canada could obtain reimbursement of pension payments covering the period of his absence.
The time has now arrived when in the view of the government there should be a much more substantial relaxation of these restrictions. Accordingly, the legislation which will be introduced upon the approval of the present resolution will provide for the following:
1.	It will do away with the present provision which requires an old age security pension to be suspended when a pensioner leaves Canada.
2.	It will substitute for the provision requiring suspension a new procedure which will permit pension payments to be continued in all cases of departure from Canada for a minimum period of six full months of absence in addition to the month in which the pensioner leaves Canada.
3.	In the case of pensioners who have resided in Canada 25 years or more after their twenty first birthday there will be no limit whatsoever on the length of the period during which they may continue to receive their pensions outside of Canada.
4.	Only in the case of pensioners who have less than 25 years of residence in Canada following their twenty first birthday will the six-month limit have any effect. Such persons, instead of having their pension suspended as soon as they leave Canada, which is the requirement under the present law, will receive their pension cheques in

the normal way for the month of their departure and will continue to have their pension cheques sent to them wherever they may be outside of Canada for a further period of absence up to a maximum of six consecutive months. If in the seventh month they return to Canada their pension payment will be paid as usual effective with the month of their return and will be continued thereafter without any interruption whatsoever. In the event, however, that they do not return to Canada before the end of the seventh month following the month of their departure from Canada, pension payments will be suspended and will be resumed only with effect from the month in which they actually return.
It will be apparent from what I have said in outlining the purposes of the new legislation that we are endeavouring by this legislation to provide substantially more generous treatment than at present to all classes of pensioners, but that we have as a particular objective the recognition of the valid claims of those long term residents of Canada who can show that they have lived the greater portion of their adult life in this country and who can therefore validly be said to have given most of the years of their life to the service of the nation. Not only have these people contributed as required under the various old age security levies during most or all of the eight years during which these levies have been in effect; but in addition to this, they may be considered to have contributed during their lengthy residence in Canada and during the bulk of their working lives to the taxes which have been required to build up and develop this country.
This group of pensioners which comprises, I may add, the vast majority of those who are presently receiving old age security benefit has, in the view of the government, and I am sure of the people of Canada, a very special claim for consideration in respect of the right to carry their pension with them for an indefinite period wherever they may move in Canada or outside of Canada following their attainment of the age of 70.
It should not be forgotten in this connection that in 1957 the government recommended, and parliament approved, an amendment to the Old Age Security Act which had the effect of reducing the residence requirement from 20 to 10 years. This means that it is possible for individuals on the basis of a relatively short period of residence in Canada to qualify for Canadian old age security benefits. It is even possible for an individual to come to Canada at the age of 60, when he has retired from active
Old Age Security Act
employment and when he may even have gone on to retirement benefit in another country, and through residence for 10 years as a retired person in Canada to claim the full benefit of old age security payments under our Canadian law.
I do not suggest that there are any grounds for questioning the right of such individuals to qualify for old age security benefit in Canada on the basis of such residence, since this is fully in accord with both the letter and the spirit of our Canadian legislation. Parliament decided in its wisdom in 1957 to make this generous provision for our older people, even for those who had newly come to Canada, and I have seen nothing in my experience with the administration of the legislation in the intervening years to suggest that this was not a wise and proper provision.
I do not think, however, that it would be expected by the Canadian people generally, or even by those who have benefited from our old age security provisions on the basis of a fairly recent arrival in Canada and a relatively short period of residence here, that they should be free after ten years' residence in Canada to return to their homelands or move to another country and take a lifetime Canadian pension with them. It seems to me. and it seems to my colleagues in the government, that while the right of a retired person to carry his old age security benefit with him wherever he goes should be recognized in principle and should be clearly enshrined in the law, it should at the same time be coupled with the principle that to qualify for such a lifetime benefit an individual should have contributed over a substantial period of years to the development of this nation and to the provision of those tax revenues which are required for the maintenance of government and services in this country, as well as the stability of the old age security fund itself.
Mr. Chairman, I think I have said enough at this stage to give the committee a fairly clear indication of the basic purposes which the amending legislation will seek to achieve if the resolution presently before the committee is given approval.
I have limited my explanations at this stage to the principal provision of the amending legislation to be introduced, but I should also mention that the bill will also contain certain purely technical provisions relating to the position of pensioners who are outside of Canada and whose pensions are therefore in suspense on the day when the new legislation will come into force. These transitional and saving provisions are of a purely technical nature, and I do not need to go into them at the present time beyond saying

Old Age Security Act
that they are intended to regularize the position of absent pensioners under the new legislation and to deal with them so far as possible as though they had been in Canada on the day when the new legislation comes into effect.
With these explanations, Mr. Chairman, I should like to commend the resolution which is now before the committee and urge its speedy approval so that we can introduce the bill itself and proceed to more detailed consideration of the various points involved at the second reading and committee stages of the bill.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING PAYMENT OF PENSION DURING ABSENCE FROM CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure that all hon. members of the committee have listened with considerable interest to the statement just made by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. I wish to assure the minister that in so far as the principle involved in this resolution is concerned it will meet with the approval of those of us in the official opposition. There will be details, of course, which we will want to examine both during this particular discussion stage and more particularly when we deal with the bill itself.
At this stage it will be desirable to confine oneself mainly to the principle of the resolution, a resolution which modifies some provisions affecting those pensioners who for one reason or another desire to leave the country. The resolution, however, is not consistent with the affirmations that were made by the government when during the course of an appeal to the people members of the government indicated their intentions of removing the restrictions in so far as foreign residence was concerned of those who were entitled under the universal. Old Age Security Act to acquire benefits. The minister has indicated in his statement the reasons for this course and in so doing has confirmed at least twice during the course of his remarks the attitude that was taken originally with regard to this particular matter when the act was introduced in 1951.
It will be remembered and noted, of course, that the Old Age Security Act is the only universal system available to any group of senior citizens in any country of the world. Many countries have different systems of providing assistance to the aged. In our country in order to eliminate what was recognized at the time as objectionable- the means test-no other course, it was thought, was open to provide for that objective than to bring in the universal system that we now have in Canada. It will be recalled, too, that the universal system was established as a result of government policy supported by a careful study that was made

of the whole problem by an all-party committee which issued a unanimous recommendation which found realization in the bill that was introduced in this house in 1951.
In order to fully appreciate some of the things that the minister has said and some of the considerations that were in contemplation at the time of introduction, it is important to know that while the present system is not a fully contributory one, it does recognize partially the principle of contribution, originally through the formula 2-2-2 and now, as the minister has mentioned 3-3-3. So, as a result, beneficiaries of this system while actually in receipt of a pension and living in Canada continue to enjoy its benefits and also have the opportunity of sharing in financial provision for the creation of the funds and the resources which make the system possible.
As the minister has said, when the present system was established there was no experience with prior contributions. No one had made any contributions to the fund at that time for the simple reason, of course, that there was no fund provided for up to that time. Therefore, in the first year it was not possible to say that any particular beneficiary had made contributions. Therefore, it would have been difficult to argue that there was, on the basis of contribution, any entitlement for beneficial enjoyment during long periods of absence or complete periods of absence from the country. Now we have had eight years of experience, and I agree with the minister the time has come when a pension having been acquired as a result of contributions and as a matter of right should entitle the pensioner to carry his or her pension outside of the country.
There will be discussion, of course, as to the restrictions which the minister proposes to see continued but with the general principle, as I said, we agree. Certainly the longer the act continues to be in existence that much greater will be the justification for the course which is being taken in principle tonight.
The minister has noted that the government itself since 1957 has moved carefully and slowly in this matter. It did not embark upon the present course in the first months of office. It wanted undoubtedly to see from experience whether or not its former or a priori declarations were sound. That the government has waited until this time is a confirmation of the course which was originally taken. As the minister said, I think quite fairly, there were quite good and valid reasons at the time for the restrictions that were imposed.
As he said, too, at the beginning, in 1952, there was no acquired right but that right

now has been acquired because the act has been in existence for almost a decade.
We were interested in listening to the outlines of what the prescribed conditions are. In the resolution these, of course, are not detailed. In the resolution which he has presented to the house the minister simply recommends to us:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Old Age Security Act to permit payment of pension in prescribed circumstances to pensioners absenting themselves from Canada beyond the period now prescribed.
The prescriptions which the minister has postulated are, if I have taken them down correctly, five in number. In the case of pensioners who have lived in Canada for 25 years there is to be no restriction whatsoever hereafter.

This is one of those rare and happy occasions when I am in a position to compliment the government on a piece of legislation that they have brought before this committee. This amendment before us today concerning old age security is something with which we have not only agreed, but something with which we have agreed for a very long time. The members of this party have for years advocated this very thing that the government has introduced today.
Just to illustrate one of those occasions, I should like to refer for a moment to Hansard for October 16, 1957, page 55, which contains the report of a speech by the former member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. M. J. Coldwell), during the throne speech debate. I quote:
May I add one other thing? I think the residential qualification should be discontinued. If a senior citizen wishes to reside perhaps in the United Kingdom or even across the line in the United States or elsewhere, the pension should be paid as of right. I say it should be paid as of right today because all the people are paying directly for it. This is no longer a gift from the treasury as it was. Right from the time a young Canadian begins to earn he is going to pay 2 per cent of his personal income tax into the social security fund. Two per cent of the corporation tax and 2 per cent of the sales tax which everybody pays also will go into that fund. Our citizens are paying a fairly substantial premium if it is considered over the working period of life of a young man or woman today. The disqualification on account of residence outside the borders of Canada should, we think,

be eliminated as well as the time for qualification reduced as is foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. It is our contention that this pension should be paid as of right.
I am very pleased, Mr. Chairman, that the government has finally introduced this measure. I must say I have to disagree with some of the remarks the minister made when he was introducing this resolution. He made reference to the fact that it is only because this is now a contributory plan that the senior citizens of this country really have any right to this pension. I think that was a very wrong picture that was painted across this country for years, because the impression was given that the pension was something from a benevolent kindhearted, good father sort of a government. Really, you are not giving your senior citizens anything when you reach in their 'back pocket, take a dollar and hand 50 cents back to them. Even when there was no direct contribution to this old age pension, it still came out of the pockets of those people who paid taxes.
I do not intend to speak very long on this resolution tonight, Mr. Chairman. However, I should like to dwell briefly on the residence clause that the minister mentioned. It is quite true that a very good financial case could be made for the fact that if a senior citizen only has to be in this country for 10 years before he can qualify for the old age security, providing he has the other qualifications, his contributions may not amount to enough to pay his pension if he returns to some other country. I think there is a matter of principle involved here, too. We are toying with a problem that has arisen before. Are we going to have two or three different kinds of Canadian citizens? Once a person has been accepted as a Canadian citizen, how can you differentiate one from another? As I say, Mr. Chairman, I am not going to deal with this matter at length tonight, but I think it is something we should keep in mind because it has risen before and I am sure it will come up again.
The minister pointed out something tonight that I think is quite significant. From the time the old age pension measure was first passed it took 20 years before there were any changes, any major amendments. Then from that time it only took nine years until there was another major amendment. Then, lo and behold, it only took three years before we got another. You can therefore see, Mr. Chairman, that the turtle of our social security program in this country is slowly starting to pick up a little bit of momentum. Maybe we can look forward to the time in the not too distant future when we can hope for improvements every year or two in our social security program.

With this hope in mind it may be that one of the other major faults in our old age security could be corrected-that correction was one that was promised by this government by a further increase of our present pension of $55 a month which in many cases is so hopelessly inadequate. The situation is hopeful for the citizens of this country if in the not too distant future our improvements start to pick up once in every one or two years instead of once in every 20 years as in the past. We can even hope that in the not too distant future we shall have a portable pension plan.

There are some people who assert that this particular measure will inspire abuses. However, this category of blind persons I feel is a category by itself. This pension is being given because of a special handicap which decreases a person's independence and increases the ordinary costs of living. I feel it has nothing to do with age. In fact, because of the infirmities of age, the blind person needs both pensions more than ever after reaching the age of 70. I would therefore ask the minister to take another look at this situation. I think it is one of the exceptions that invariably surround every rule. Certainly the government will deserve the approbation of the country for improving the Old Age Security Act. But I ask hon. members to recognize at the same time that it was the former government which introduced this legislation. It may have had defects. Perhaps it did not meet all the anticipations. The minister's present proposal is nothing new. I should like to point out that when the matter first came up in 1951 I spoke on this bill at the time. I should like to indicate that I dealt with section 5 on that occasion and suggested that consideration should be given to old age pensioners who wished to live outside the country. I made that suggestion to the minister at the time, and proposed that it be incorporated in the bill. But reasons were given, as the minister made clear tonight, why it could not then be done. I should like to read part of what I said then on November 26, 1951. I am reading from Hansard of 1951 at page 1319:
The Minister of National Health and Welfare has frankly stated during the debate that time and experience may suggest improvements.
It is logical that that should happen.
At the risk of being redundant I want to ask the minister again to review section 5 of the act which deals with the suspension of the pension to anyone who leaves Canada for a certain period.
Thus the minister's present proposal is nothing new; it is not a new discovery. The point was raised before, though it was not put into effect for reasons which the minister has explained. I hope hon. members opposite will

have the courtesy to recognize that this legislation was enacted by the former government and not by the present government. Of course, as time goes on situations change and improvements are possible. The financial status of people changes. It is not a stroke of genius on the part of the minister, but a natural development of the circumstances of our time.

Perhaps $100 a month is not feasible in the opinion of the government. Perhaps the economic situation does not justify it. They may some time be asked, why they did not make it $60 or $75, and the answer would be that circumstances did not permit it at that time. This was a most desirable piece of legislation when it was introduced. The whole country welcomed it. Why did not the opposition at that time make these proposals, if they say they would like them in the bill? As a matter of fact, a government supporter made that suggestion to the minister. I said as reported at page 1319 of Hansard of November 26, 1951:
At the age of 70 and over people become quite frail, and frequently they are alone. They may have to leave Canada for short or long periods to preserve their health or in order to reside with a child outside of Canada rather than live with strangers or alone. If the denial of the monthly pension is to produce real hardship, the minister, I know, will have another look at this section of the act with a view to eliminating such a possibility.
The time has properly come. This government made certain promises to the people of Canada and the times now permit their present action. As I said, the cost of living has increased and the government goes forward, and eliminates a hardship which we at that time could not eliminate because of circumstances. I say very frankly that I recognize favourably the move which the government is now making. This is something which was promised; something which will stand up and be of real use. I dare say that when the bill is presented we may have further improvements to suggest. The government may reply that it cannot go quite as far as we would like in present circumstances.

That is quite possible. It is the kind of debate which does take place. But I ask hon. members who support the government to give due credit where it belongs for bringing in this legislation in the first place.
I find it necessary now to read a part of the speech made by the former minister of national health and welfare when he introduced this bill in 1951. At that time, the hon. member for Essex East said this:
Mr. Speaker, the bill now under consideration is part of Canada's new program for old age security, climaxing a quarter century of progress in this field.
The government's twofold plan for old age assistance and universal pensions represents the greatest single advance made in this country in our provisions for senior Canadians. It is a national vote of confidence in Canada's capacity to provide for the security of its older citizens.
That is the spirit which prevailed at that time. Certainly we welcomed it and the measure was unanimously adopted.
With regard to the resolution itself, may I say that the experience of the past eight years has revealed certain hardships and difficulties. Certainly the civil servants who administer the act have been very loyal and shown themselves very able, but they have often been confronted with difficulties and circumstances in which understanding is required. One of these difficulties stems from the fact that in many cases it is far from easy for our senior citizens to give satisfactory proof of age. That has been one of the complaints which I have encountered and which I am sure the department has encountered. In my own experience I have found very sympathetic understanding shown by the deputy minister and the senior officials in helping to solve the problems of people who have come to this country late in life after the destruction of records in Europe which would normally have provided proof of age.
A similar difficulty may arise with regard to showing proof of the date on which a person arrived in Canada, how long a person has lived in Canada and what interpretation may be given to the requirement of 25 years residence. Will that phrase mean 25 years consistent and continual residence in Canada, or will some allowance be made if an old age pensioner has been absent, say for a year or two, or for six months, during that period? I am wondering whether any hardship is likely to arise from the wording of the bill. I hope the minister will say that the provision does not necessarily mean 25 years continuous residence in the country.
I hope the minister and the government will approach this and similar problems with sympathy and understanding, and I hope
Old Age Security Act
this attitude will extend to whatever improvements we may be able to suggest to what I have no hesitation in calling a laudable piece of legislation. I am sure, too, that hon. members opposite who have asked why every possible provision was not inserted in the original act will now have-I will not say the courage-the desire and the intention of endeavouring to encompass everything of a constructive and useful nature which might lead to an improvement on the present resolution which the minister has put forward.

Mr. Chairman, I listened to the hon. member for Essex East with the same delight that many other hon. members of the committee experienced in listening to his oh so brief remarks as he brought to our attention the various sequences of thought which flickered across his mind, most of them completely irrelevant to the topic under discussion and the resolution before the committee.
I should like in what I hope will be a brief manner to say that I feel this resolution should be treated with a great deal of concern and speed. Rather than listening to recitations of past honours deserved or undeserved let us forget the baloney, take a look at the resolution itself and bear in mind for just a moment what the government has in mind which is to benefit the senior citizens of this nation.
I suggest that we vote upon this resolution promptly, save the time of the committee and at the same time bring a benefit to the senior citizens of this country.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am going to be brief but I cannot resist getting up to express my support for the spirit, the principle and the purpose of this resolution. It is an amendment that has been urged upon former governments and this government by this group for many years. We are pleased to see the amendment which will mean so much to particular groups of our older citizens, those who require for health reasons to live in other countries perhaps to lengthen their lives and those who wish to return to their old country to live with family or friends.
In discussing a resolution of this type I not only see the resolution on the order paper and listen to the details of the debate but in my mind's eye I see the number of people in Canada who will be assisted by the resolution. I am sure we all rejoice in this opportunity.
I listened to the hon. member for Essex East with pleasure keeping my weather eye open to see what was coming next. I heard his reference to the Clark report and the intimation that the government should have hastened in

We in this group know where we stand. We hope the government will take action in the near future to develop in Canada an overall comprehensive national pension scheme to meet the needs of our citizens in their retirement years. 10. Agricultural Stabilization Act administration, $315,130.

Mr. Chairman, may I ask the minister if he is in a position to announce whether or not there will be a floor price on sugar beets? If he is not in a position to make that announcement can the minister say when he hopes to be in that position? When dealing with that perhaps the minister could tell us about my concern and that of other farmers in Ontario-
Oh, oh.

-as to when we may have some announcement with regard to a floor price on Ontario grown wheat, and also whether or not it is the intention of the minister to provide for a support price on wheat outside of the stabilization act.

Mr. Chairman, when dealing with this matter last Friday I announced that there would be a price announced for sugar beets in the near future. That is the situation. I expect it will be announced in a few days' time. The same thing applies to the other commodities. An announcement will be made shortly concerning both wheat and soy beans.

Can the minister say whether or not the government proposes before the end of this session or between the end of this session and the beginning of

the next to withdraw the support principle under this act and provide some other system of assistance as it did in the case of hogs and eggs?

I also stated last Friday that we would continue to support the maximum number of agricultural commodities as the necessity for that support arose by whatever means was most appropriate for the support, whether by means of deficiency payments, offer to purchase, flat payments or some other means.

What the minister is saying is that we will be confronted sometime during this session or the next with further repudiations by the government of its price support policy under the Agricultural Stabilization Act?

Mr. Chairman, this constant reiteration on the part of the hon. member for Essex East of words like "repudiation" and references along that line is something of which I am sure all hon. members of this committee have grown tired particularly when references of that kind have absolutely no foundation in fact. There has been no repudiation at any time as far as agricultural policy or the stabilization act is concerned. We have provided to the farmers of this country support on a larger number of commodities under the stabilization act than exists in most other countries of the world and so many more commodities than the former government of which the hon. gentleman was a member that there is no comparison. The government of which he was a member only in one year supported more than six commodities and the only time it did so was during the epidemic of foot-and-mouth disease. Apart from that, four commodities were the most they ever supported in any one year. Since we passed the stabilization act we have had over 20 commodities under support at all times.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, may I be allowed to say a few words on the stabilization of agricultural prices, particularly with regard to sheep and lambs.
We know, first of all, that on May 8, 1959, the agricultural prices stabilization board had announced a support price of $19.55 per hundredweight, in Toronto, for live lambs graded "good". In September of the same year, the board decided to buy from the packers lamb carcasses, graded "Canada choice" and "Canada good", which had been stored by the packers. In October 1959, the same board issued a release in which it

indicated its intention to purchase frozen lamb from the same organizations.
The first requirement of the board, was that to be eligible for purchase the lambs had to be slaughtered and graded in a registered slaughter-house, one in which there was official inspection and grading by the Department of Agriculture. Now we have in Canada small slaughter-houses, operated by individuals, that cannot share in the benefits of this legislation because they are not inspected.
I have received complaints from some of those individuals operating small abattoirs, and not eligible for the benefits of this legislation. Therefore, I ask the minister whether he intends to amend the board's regulations so that those small operators may share in the benefits of this legislation, in view of the fact that the regulations of the prices stabilization board, such as they now exist, discriminate against small operators.
That is so true that I have received a letter from an Ontario gentleman, from which I should like to quote a few words. The letter is signed by a Mr. Robinson, of Hannon, Ontario. I quote:
(Text):
The problem as presented by Mr. Robinson to me is that this subsidy which at the present time amounts to approximately nine cents a pound is not available to him since he runs a small slaughterhouse. Although he advises that he does have Ontario government inspection, he is not set up to accommodate federal inspection in his packing plant.
Mr. Robinson cannot benefit from this recommendation.
(Translation):
Since this man's facilities are not inspected by the federal Department of Agriculture, he is unable to enjoy the same privileges as the large slaughter-houses. I therefore ask the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) whether he intends to change the regulations so that our small businessmen may take advantage of the legislation and continue to operate.
(Text):

Mr. Chairman, the regulations to which the hon. member refers really are health regulations. They are in effect for the protection of the Canadian public as far as the quality of the meat which they buy is concerned. Only meat that has been killed in inspected establishments, that is establishments which meet certain standards, can enter into interprovincial trade, and it is only from establishments of that kind, of course, that the stabilization board purchases meats of any
Supp ly-A griculture
kind, whether sheep, pork, or whatever it may.
If we did not do that we would be in the position of being unable to ship the meat that we purchase to any place where the market happens to exist, or ship it out of the country, or to any place else. It would be a completely impractical operation. The actual fact is that owing to our purchase of whatever meat is surplus from the inspected slaughtering plants, it means that the smaller slaughtering plants which have not met the standards of inspection have the ability to sell into a market which they would not have otherwise and are able to dispose of their products. Therefore, actually they suffer from no disadvantage at all.
(Translation):

Controls by the price stabilization board are a handicap to those small producers because those producers cannot afford to pay the same prices as the operators of large slaughter-houses. I feel, therefore, that such control is discriminatory against small producers, small businessmen, and operators of medium-sized slaughter-houses. Some of them might slaughter as many as 50 sheep every week; their slaughter-house is inspected by provincial officials, but they cannot take advantage of the legislation. As a result, they have to pay nine or ten cents more a pound for their lambs than the operators of large packing plants. That is why I suggest that this control is prejudical to small business and to small producers.
(Text):
Mr. Chairman, once more I am afraid the hon. member does not understand the situation.
Yes, I understand.

The price at which sheep or hogs are sold and so on, whether they are bought by a smaller packing plant or a large packing plant, is determined by the support price when the price of sheep is down to the support level. That is what determines the price of live lambs and the wholesale price of lamb products that are sold by small plants is determined in this way. The result, as I say, is that any surplus that exists is taken off the market by the stabilization board and the small plant is able to get the same price as the bigger plant, putting its product out into retail outlets or into wholesale outlets, except for the fact that some wholesalers will not buy uninspected meat because they cannot ship it across interprovincial boundaries and in some cities they are not allowed to sell it. The remedy for these small plants that the hon. member has mentioned is to bring the standards of their establishments up to the

Supply-Agriculture
health standards which we set so that they will be able to pass federal inspection.
How much would it cost to have federal inspection? I have a letter here which says it would cost half a million dollars to secure the equipment in order to qualify for such inspection.
It costs absolutely nothing for federal inspection. We supply it free of charge.
It is the equipment.

The concern has to bring its operations up to specified health standards which we must maintain if we are going to be able to send our meats into export markets, across interprovincial boundaries and into some cities which fortunately, I think, have pretty strict inspection facilities. Actually what the hon. member is requesting is that we should relax our health standards as far as the inspection and sale of meat are concerned. This simply means that what he is asking is that we should give our blessing to the possible sale of diseased or other inferior meat to the general public which of course we cannot do.

In our province we have classification inspection but we do not have health inspection. I do not know about the other provinces but in Quebec we do not have health inspection and nobody has died from any meat produced there.

Mr. Chairman, item 10 is one where the minister might give the committee some information as to the quantity of pork that has been handled by the board, the quantity of pork purchased from time to time in the recent past, some idea of the prices that have been paid for the various cuts of pork, the quantity involved, and some of the main companies that have handled this pork on government account, if the minister has that information. I am particular interested in the business transaction that was carried out whereby I believe some of this pork was sold back to the packing companies from whom it had been purchased. I am interested in the price which these packing companies paid to the agricultural stabilization board for what I believe to have been very large quantities of pork resold to the companies.

Mr. Chairman, I gave figures last Friday, which are to be found at page 3885 of Hansard, as to the amount of pork which we held in the form of frozen pork, as canned luncheon meat and as canned hams as of March 31 of this year. As far as total purchases are concerned, I cannot give complete figures except to say that altogether

we purchased in the neighbourhood of 126,870,000 pounds of pork cuts of one kind and another. Some of this was sold back to be canned as canned pork and then we took possession after it was canned. Some of it was sold into the market. A certain amount was exported and some was put into canned hams. Therefore there is an overlap in the figures from that point of view. However, I think the inventory at the end of March is as definite a figure as I can give at the moment, and I have indicated that I gave that information last Friday.
With respect to the prices at which the various pork cuts have been sold, these have varied considerably. I have not got a list of the figures here. A return was asked for some time ago and I believe that return was tabled and is now part of the records of the house. The return shows what the costs and so on were. The return is about an inch thick.
Do you have the number of the return?
I have not the number of the return. As I recall, the return was asked for by a member of the C.C.F. party. I have forgotten just who it was but I believe it was a member of your group.
It included figures of quantities of pork purchased?

As I say, it is a very voluminous return; it is about an inch thick. There have been thousands and thousands of entries with regard to the handling of pork and therefore when the hon. member asks for figures it is a very difficult thing to give specific figures because there have been so many transactions in both purchases and sales. As the hon. member will realize, we were buying all this pork in the form of fresh pork cuts and we were not able to find storage space for all of it. Therefore we had to start canning it and what we did in a large number of cases was to buy fresh pork cuts, turn them back to an abattoir for canning and pay a canning fee on the pork. That really involved many cases of what one might call book entries.
We bought pork and we sold it back to the canning companies and then bought the canned pork from them. Actually what we were really doing was paying them for the canning.
What was the price received for pork bellies when they were sold back to the companies for canning purposes?

We did not sell any bellies to the companies for canning purposes. You cannot can bellies. As the hon. member is

aware, bellies are chiefly fat and if you attempt to can bellies all you really get is a can of lard with a small amount of meat in it. Therefore no bellies were sold back for canning purposes.
Were bellies sold back to the companies?
Bellies were sold untinned to the highest tenderer for rendering into lard.
Can the minister give us first of all the prices paid for the bellies; second, the quantities involved; and, third, the prices received for them?

I have not the figures here that the hon. member has mentioned. I think they appear in the return to which I have referred, and all I can say is that if they are not there I will be very glad to supply them. Generally speaking, of course, we took a severe loss on bellies. There is no question about that because, as I say, once you have pork in the freezer for a certain length of time it tends to get what is known as freezer burn. You can hold it in storage only for a certain length of time. After these bellies particularly had been held for a certain length of time in cold storage we were completely unable to sell them either in Canada or abroad and we had to take some kind of action to salvage as much food value as we could. The only thing we could do was to sell them for rendering into lard which we did. I cannot recall offhand what the amount sold for this purpose was. We did dispose of a limited number of bellies overseas but otherwise they were sold for rendering into lard. We still hold quite a number of bellies and we hope we will be able to dispose of them either on the home market or abroad at not too great a loss. But with respect to the older ones which we bought at the beginning of the purchase program we had to, as I say, salvage what we could out of them and we did that in the only way it could be done, by selling them for rendering purposes.

Mr. Chairman, it puts the committee in a very difficult position when the minister does not have the information with him to answer the questions we ask. My information, obtained from some people in Edmonton-this is why I want some information from the minister-is that very large quantities of pork bellies were purchased by the board from packing companies at relatively good prices. They were sold back to the same packing companies from which they had been purchased in the first place, but they were sold back at such low prices as to be almost a donation to those packing
Supply-Agriculture
companies. The feeling of the people who were talking to me was that the packing companies in the city of Edmonton had made a killing in this business and that the government and the stabilization board had really been taken in, and that this constituted a very substantial cost to the federal treasury.
I do not want to make assertions; I do not want to hurl accusations. I am trying to get some information from the minister on this item on these particular points. Since there are many millions of dollars involved I feel the committee has a right to ask for this information and to receive it before this item passes. I do not believe it is good enough when we are asked to look up returns in the house or when we are told we can get the information tabled at a later time. I think we should have this information when this item is being discussed.

As I said, there is no question whatever of not providing all the information which it is possible to provide. The point I made before was that the information the hon. member requested could not be given here. If I were to give all of it we would be two days on this one subject because it constitutes thousands of entries. I say there is a very thick return in connection with it and these details can be looked up.
So far as the assertion about which the hon. member spoke and which he said had been made that the packing companies have made a killing in connection with these bellies, that is completely incorrect. We had one or two cases of people who bought these bellies on tender and who attempted to put the bellies back into the trade by selling them as bacon. Those people were promptly prosecuted. As a matter of fact, it cost them a considerable amount of money, rather than making a killing, to attempt to do it. We exercise very close supervision over the disposal of these bellies and we made sure that they were converted into lard. The prices that were paid for them were fairly low. As the hon. member probably knows, the price of lard is extremely low. Certainly, there was no killing made by the people who bought these and converted them into lard.

I ask the minister to bring to this committee, before this item passes some information, the information I have requested or enough of the information to give the committee a picture of what has happened. His officials are before him. It is the ordinary practice to ask the administration for details at this time. This is what the estimates are for. There are many millions of dollars involved, and for the minister to come in here empty-handed, without any information, is scarcely good enough.

Supply-Agriculture
I am going to insist, it the discussion should appear to determinate before ten o'clock, that this item stand until the minister can bring to the committee the information I have been requesting. This item is the whole basis of the government's support program which is under attack in the country, which I think has been a disservice to the agricultural producers of this country, which has cost the taxpayers a great deal of money and is doing nothing at the moment, in the opinion of organized agriculture on the prairies, except to cause hardship and to bring about a great deal of uncertainty in the agriculture industry. I believe the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska has some questions to ask. If he has not, I shall continue, but certainly we are entitled to this information and I hope we will get it.

Mr. Chairman, as I said, we are quite willing and anxious to give any information which is requested. I am not clear what information the hon. member wants. As he put his question in the first instance I would have been required to be reading here for a very, very long time. The transactions which have taken place, as I have said before, have been thousands in number. What he asked was the price at which these pork cuts had been bought, and the price at which they had been sold.
Some general idea.
If he would make it clear exactly what information he wants, I shall be glad to get it. As I say, I am not clear as to what information he does want.

Then I would ask the minister to provide this committee, beginning January 1, 1959, with the monthly totals of pork products that have been purchased under this act; the average price that was paid per month for the various cuts involved. I should like the average price that has been paid for the bellies that have been sold. I should like the average price that has been obtained from the companies, and I should like some indication of the largest purchases that have been made by some of the packing companies in the country. I should like the minister to supply the committee with the lowest tender price received by the government for the pork bellies which, according to the minister, have gone into the production of lard.
I just want a general picture of the operations of this board. Surely that can be done. The minister does not have to produce every single transaction; that is not the information we want. This committee is entitled, and I think the minister would be able to do it, to an outline to date of the general operations of the board, the general prices it has been

paying from time to time, the prices it has been receiving from time to time and the cost to the treasury. Let us have enough information to find out how well these packing companies have done on their purchases.

As I said, I will be glad to secure this information. I do not know whether it can all be secured in exactly the form in which the hon. member has requested it. If not, and if anybody really wants to go into this in detail, I think the best way to do it is to study the return of which I spoke. One of my officials tells me it has not been filed as yet. It went through my office three or four days ago.
You are now talking about something we have not got.

I am always frank and honest with this committee. The hon. member is now trying to insinuate that I was trying to mislead this committee when I said this return had been made. It passed through my office several days ago, and I approved it. I thought it had been filed. My official says he does not think it has been filed. Why it has not, I do not know. In any event, that was the situation.
The point I am making is that if anyone wants to go into this in detail, it will be a matter of several days study going over these figures. In so far as a general picture is concerned, I will attempt to give as good a general picture as possible along the lines the hon. member has requested to the committee tomorrow morning.

I thank the minister for the conclusion of his answer. It is a little difficult for a member of the committee to be told over a period of 10 minutes that a large file has been tabled, a voluminous one that contains all the information that we are requesting and all we have to do is study it. I sent out for the return as soon as the minister mentioned it, and I am waiting to see whether or not the sessional papers office produces it. The minister has now said that he is not certain whether or not the sessional papers office does, in fact, have the return. It is therefore rather difficult for the members of the committee to deal with the problem when we are not even sure whether or not the return has been tabled and is available to hon. members.
Since the lifting of the embargo on imports from the United States can the minister tell us what quantities of hogs and hog products have been imported?

I do not know the exact quantity but it has been almost negligible. A few trial shipments, small in quantity,

were sent over from the United States but they did not go very well. Apparently there was no profit in them and apparently there were no repeat orders. The prices in Canada and in the United States, when you take into consideration the duty, the cost of transportation and particularly the difference in quality, have been such that as to the shipment of United States pork over here since the embargo was removed, the possibility of it just really has not existed.
Can the minister give us the figures tomorrow?

Yes, we can give the figure tomorrow, but I do not think the figure is material because, as I say, the quantities are extremely small. The total volume of imported pork, particularly in comparison with what we use ourselves and what we ship to the United States is just negligible.
For the information of the committee I may say that I have received a note from the page. I take it that it is from the sessional papers office. It is unsigned but it reads as follows:

We have nothing on pork purchases for this year.
This shows just how difficult it is to discuss this question when the minister tells us to look at a return that is not yet available. I hope that by eleven o'clock tomorrow this return will be made available. The minister said it will not be much good to us because it is going to take many days to study it. This is not a very satisfactory method by which to deal with the minister's estimates. He promised-and I know he will keep his promise-that tomorrow he will have available for us in summary form some of the information we have been requesting with regard to the details of the operations of the stabilization board. Therefore tomorrow we can continue with these questions on the basis of the information we are given at that time.

I have another question to ask the minister and if he cannot supply the answer to this question tonight, I will ask him to supply it for tomorrow. How many farmers are registered to receive the support price on hogs or what number of farmers or percentage of farmers or hog producers have received or are eligible for the support price?

We will have that information tomorrow morning also. I think the committee realizes the fact that with the magnitude of the operations of the stabilization board, the statistics required to answer many questions of this sort would constitute an extraordinarily big pile, that this is not a
Supply-Agriculture
matter on which an hon. member can ask a question and I or the officials can produce an answer instantaneously. In a large number of cases it is something with regard to which we require some notice so that we can have the files looked up and find the answer.
(Translation):

Could the minister tell us whether legal action was taken against farmers who took advantage of the Agricultural Stabilization Act under two registration numbers?
I stated some time ago that certain farmers were using two registration numbers. Therefore, I ask the minister whether legal action was taken by the Department of Agriculture.
(Text):

I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, but I do not understand what the hon. member was talking about. Possibly the translation was not very good. Certainly I did not catch from it anything to which I could make a reply.

speechtext: The hon. member for Drum-mond-Arthabaska has a question that has not been answered because I think the minister stated that the translation was not too clear.

I just could not get anything which I could understand through the translation system. I would suggest that the best thing for me to do, inasmuch as this item is going to be allowed to stand, is to read in Hansard tomorrow what the question was and then give the answer at that time.
Before this item is allowed to stand, I should like to know whether anybody else besides the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska will be allowed to put his questions tomorrow. I am prepared to speak.
Go ahead.

I am prepared to speak. The hon. member for Assiniboia went

S upp ly-A gricu Iture
to great lengths last Friday to condemn the policy of deficiency payments on hogs and to condemn the stabilization board for the reduction of the support price for hogs. At no time did he offer any solution and at no time did he state that he knew of a better method than a support price for hogs. All he did was to condemn.
There should be a floor price.

There is a floor price now, and the hon. member knows very well how the floor price works. He went to great pains to point out what was wrong with it. But as to how to improve it, he mentioned nothing. He stated that production had increased and he thought that perhaps this increase resulted from the floor price being too high. I do not know whether or not he mentioned that. There was some reason for the increase. One reason for the production of hogs being as high as it was last year was that there was a surplus of grain to quite an extent three years ago on the prairies. The farmers were anxious to move this grain, and hogs provided an ideal outlet. They therefore went into the production of hogs.
The hon. member for Drummond-Artha-baska stated that because our pork exports were falling off we were going to be in a drastic situation with regard to pork surpluses, even with the present method of support.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I inquire what the business is for tomorrow and for next week as well?

speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: For tomorrow we will continue with the estimates of the Department of Agriculture followed by those of the post office. On Monday and Tuesday there will be a supply motion. On Wednesday we have available for the consideration of the house the budget resolutions; No. 11 on today's order paper which is the resolution in the name of the Minister of Veterans Affairs with regard to War Veterans Act; then No. 6 on today's order paper which is the resolution in the name of the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys concerning the Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act; and No. 3 on today's order paper which is second reading of Bill No. S-27, an act to control and regulate the sale of feed. Thursday and Friday of next week will be available for estimates and we will have for those two days the two departments that I have called for tomorrow, if they are not completed, followed by the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys and the Department of Transport.
At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put pursuant to standing order.
The following answers, deposited with the Clerk of the house, are printed in the official report of debates pursuant to standing order 39:

subsubtopic: PERSONNEL
speechtext:
